name: Headache
source_guidance: Adapted from NHS 111 guidance on headaches, WHO guidance on meningitis and stroke, and WHO recommendations on pre-eclampsia warning signs in pregnancy.

questions.text: Is the person unconscious, very drowsy, confused, or having a fit?
Did a very severe headache start suddenly, like a blow to the head, or is it the worst headache ever?
Is there a stiff neck with fever, or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it?
Is there new weakness, numbness, face drooping, slurred speech, or loss of vision?
Is the person pregnant or recently gave birth, with blurred vision, swelling of the face or hands, or pain under the ribs?
Did the headache start after a head injury, or is the person on blood-thinning medicine?
Is there a fever with the headache?
Have the headaches been getting more frequent or worse over several weeks?

emergency: Call 112 now, or get to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately.
Note the time the headache started.
Lay the person on their side if drowsy or vomiting.
Do not drive yourself. Ask someone to take you, or wait for the ambulance.
urgent: Go to a hospital or clinic today.
If there is fever, ask for a malaria test.
Do not drink alcohol and avoid strong painkillers until seen.
Call 112 if the person becomes confused, drowsy, or develops weakness or a stiff neck.
routine: Book a clinic appointment within the next few days and ask for a blood pressure check.
Keep a headache diary: when it happens, how long, and what helps.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
self_care: Rest in a quiet, dark room and drink plenty of water.
Paracetamol can be taken as directed on the pack. Do not take painkillers on more than a few days a week.
Eat regular meals and get enough sleep.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
